column2: For a continuous random variable, what is \(P(X = x)\)?
column3: Zero, for every \(x\): probability lives in intervals, not points.

column2: A density has height 3 at some point. Is the probability of that point 3?
column3: No. The density is a rate of accumulation; only its integral over an interval is a probability.

column2: What two conditions must a density satisfy?
column3: \(f(x) \ge 0\) everywhere, and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\).

column2: How do the CDF and the density relate?
column3: \(F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)\,du\) and \(f(x) = F'(x)\) — the density is the slope of the CDF.

column2: Can a density exceed 1? Give a case.
column3: Yes. \(\mathrm{Unif}(0, 0.5)\) has density 2 on its support, which integrates to 1 over a width of one half.

column2: Why is \(P(a \le X \le b) = P(a < X < b)\) for a continuous variable?
column3: Because the endpoints are single points and each carries probability zero, so including or excluding them changes nothing.

column2: What are the mean and variance of \(\mathrm{Unif}(a,b)\)?
column3: Mean \((a+b)/2\), variance \((b-a)^2/12\).

column2: Why can the uniform distribution on \([0,1]\) not be justified by the naive definition?
column3: Because the interval is uncountable, so there is no finite sample space to count; only the axioms of countable additivity can assign it probabilities.

column2: Write the standardisation formula and say what it buys you.
column3: \(z = (x-\mu)/\sigma\); it converts any normal into the standard normal, so one table serves every normal distribution.

column2: \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(2, 0.5^2)\). Standardise \(x = 2.6\).
What fraction of a normal distribution lies within one, two and three standard deviations?
Given \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), how do you build a \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) variable?
column3: \(X = \mu + \sigma Z\) — the location-scale construction.

column2: Write the exponential density and state its mean and variance in terms of \(\lambda\).
column3: \(f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x \ge 0\); mean \(1/\lambda\), variance \(1/\lambda^2\).

column2: State memorylessness as an equation.
column3: \(P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)\) for all \(s, t \ge 0\).

column2: With \(\lambda = 0.5\), what is \(P(X > 3)\), and what is \(P(X > 7 \mid X > 4)\)?
column3: Both are \(e^{-1.5} \approx 0.223\), which is the point of memorylessness.

column2: Which discrete distribution is the exponential's counterpart, and what is the shared property?
column3: The Geometric; both are memoryless, with \(P(X>n) = (1-p)^n\) and \(P(X>t) = e^{-\lambda t}\).

column2: For i.i.d. continuous \(X, Y\), what is \(P(X < Y)\) and why?
column3: \(1/2\), by symmetry, with \(P(X = Y) = 0\) so the two strict orderings exhaust the probability.

column2: Why is the probability of a tie zero, and when does that stop being true?
column3: Single points carry probability zero for a continuous variable; discretising or rounding gives ties positive probability.

column2: Three i.i.d. continuous draws. What is the probability that \(X_1\) is the smallest?
column3: \(1/3\) — all six orderings are equally likely.

column2: State the universality of the uniform, and give the one-line proof.
column3: If \(U \sim \mathrm{Unif}(0,1)\) then \(F^{-1}(U)\) has CDF \(F\), because \(P(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = P(U \le F(x)) = F(x)\).

column2: What is the inverse-CDF formula for the exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda\)?
column3: \(X = -\ln(U)/\lambda\), using that \(1-U\) is also uniform.

column2: \(\lambda = 2\), \(U = 0.3\). What is the sample, and how do you check it?
How does inverse-CDF sampling produce a token from a language model?
column3: Draw \(U\) uniformly, walk the cumulative probabilities of the softmax output until you pass \(U\), and emit that token — the same construction with a finite support.

column2: If \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon\), what is the distribution of \(z\)?
column3: \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) — the location-scale family.

column2: \(\mu = 1\), \(\sigma = 0.5\), \(\varepsilon = -1.2\). What is \(z\)?
Why does the reparameterized form admit gradients when a direct draw does not?
column3: Because \(z\) becomes an ordinary differentiable expression in \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), with the randomness in an independent \(\varepsilon\) outside the parameters.

column2: Which kind of distribution resists reparameterization, and what does that force you to do?
column3: Discrete ones such as the categorical; you must use a relaxation (or the score-function estimator) instead of an exact differentiable transform.

column2: Why is the isotropic Gaussian prior what makes the VAE's KL term a sum over coordinates?
column3: Because \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\) factorises across coordinates, so the divergence separates into one independent term per latent dimension.

column2: Write the diffusion forward process and say which construction from this essay it is.
column3: \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\) — reparameterization of a Gaussian, a scaled signal plus scaled standard noise.

column2: Why does diffusion's training objective depend on the sample being a formula rather than a black-box draw?
column3: Because the same \(\varepsilon\) can then serve as a known regression target, which turns the bound into a supervised denoising problem.

column2: Why is a Gaussian a reasonable prior but a poor model for images?
column3: It is the maximum-entropy choice given a mean and variance and is closed under the needed operations, but it is not what image pixels look like; a fixed-variance Gaussian decoder is usually the weakest part of a VAE.
